```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.pos = "htbp")
template_dir <- "../../_shared/template"
source(file.path(template_dir, "viscount_rmd_helpers.R"))
library(jsonlite)

read_json5_clean <- function (arg0_path) {
  txt <- readLines(arg0_path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  txt <- paste(txt, collapse = "\n")
  txt <- gsub("//[^\n]*", "", txt)
  txt <- gsub("/\\*.*?\\*/", "", txt)
  txt <- gsub(",\\s*([}\\]])", "\\1", txt)
  fromJSON(txt, simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json5_clean("gojoseon_commanderies_and_three_kingdoms.json5")
sett_data <- fromJSON("gojoseon_commanderies_and_three_kingdoms_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
ledger_data <- read_json5_clean("gojoseon_commanderies_and_three_kingdoms_source_ledger.json5")

reg_names <- c(
  pyongan_taedong_lelang_goguryeo = "Pyongan-Taedong",
  hamgyong_okjeo_tumen = "Hamgyong-Tumen",
  hwanghae_daifang_imjin = "Hwanghae-Imjin",
  han_geum_baekje_core = "Han-Geum Basin",
  yeongsan_honam_tamna = "Yeongsan-Honam",
  nakdong_gaya_south = "Lower Nakdong",
  gyeongbuk_silla_core = "Gyeongbuk-Gyeongju",
  gangwon_dongye_taebaek = "Gangwon-Dongye"
)
```

# Abstract

This gazetteer catalogues 209 urban citadels, administrative commandery seats, mountain redoubts and market settlements active across the Korean Peninsula between 250BC and 668AD (covering 226.901 km² across eight macro-regional territorial units). Synthesising documentary records from the Samguk Sagi, Samguk Yusa, Hanshu Dilizhi and Sanguozhi alongside extensive Korean salvage archaeological excavations and mortuary tumuli surveys [@Barnes2015Archaeology; @Nelson2017Mumun; @Hong2018Cultural; @Lee2016Bioanthropological], the register encompasses the primary administrative seats and royal capitals of early Korean history: the dual metropolises of Pyongyang (180k) and Gyeongju (180k), the successive Baekje capitals of Seoul (75k), Gongju (55k) and Buyeo (85k), the ceremonial complex of Iksan (38k), the maritime entrepôt of Gimhae (35k), the Chinese commandery headquarters of Daifang (28k), and the Gaya highland citadel of Goryeong (26k). Across the 209 catalogued entries, the gazetteer records 685 settlement-year population observations spanning 250BC to 668AD (averaging 3,28 observations per centre). In the regional source ledger, 507 candidate entities were evaluated and consolidated as duplicate historical aliases and close-pair suburban sites out of 716 total evaluated candidates, maintaining zero unaccounted entries.

# Background

Settlement morphology in early historical Korea was shaped by the strategic requirements of mountain defense, riverine agricultural transport and royal palace administration [@Barnes2015Archaeology; @Nelson2017Mumun]. During the Bronze and Early Iron Age Mumun transition, settlements evolved from open river-terrace pit-house hamlets into nucleated hilltop villages protected by defensive ditches and wooden palisades (*hwanho chirak*) [@Choe2002Mumun; @Barnes2015Archaeology].

With the introduction of iron metallurgy and the establishment of Wiman Joseon and the Han commanderies (Lelang and Daifang), urban architecture adopted Chinese ram-earth (*hangto*) wall construction techniques, monumental tiled roofs and formal administrative layouts [@Barnes2015Archaeology]. Throughout the Three Kingdoms era, Korean states developed a distinctive dual-fortress defense system: kings and civilian populations resided in peacetime lowland walled cities or earthen palaces (such as Pungnaptoseong in Hanseong, Anhak Palace in Pyongyang, or Wolseong in Gyeongju), paired with adjacent upland stone mountain fortresses (*sanseong*, such as Mongchontoseong, Daeseongsanseong, Gongsanseong, Busosanseong and Myeonghwalsanseong) where garrisons retreated during siege warfare [@Barnes2015Archaeology; @Hong2018Cultural].

# Methodology

Settlement records were constructed by extracting verified archaeological citadels, commandery county seats and dynastic capitals from national excavation gazetteers and harmonising them with historical demographic estimates from Kwon and Shin (1977), Barnes (2015) and regional survey corpora [@Barnes2015Archaeology; @KwonShin1977Joseon; @Nelson2017Mumun]. All 209 catalogued settlements carry verified historical coordinates and assign to one of the eight macro-regional masks.

In the regional source ledger, 507 candidate records were excluded as duplicate historical aliases, close-pair suburban entities situated within 8 km of primary walled citadels, or temporary campaign encampments lacking sustained civilian settlement [@Barnes2015Archaeology]. For example, historical aliases such as Wanggeom-seong, Lelang, Nangnang and Janganseong were consolidated into Pyongyang; Geumseong and Saro were consolidated into Gyeongju; Sabi and Soburi were consolidated into Buyeo; and Wiryeseong, Hanseong and Pungnap were consolidated into Seoul.

# Testing and Validation

Ledger reconciliation confirms 209 included settlements and 507 excluded candidate entries (716 total evaluated entities, with zero unaccounted records). All 209 settlements carry WGS84 geographic coordinates and documented population observations across the ten peninsular benchmarks. Figure \ref{fig:sett-gazetteer} displays the rank-size distribution and the leading fortified urban centres of the peninsula.

# Results

## Top 45 Settlements by Peak Population

Table \ref{tab:top45-korea} presents the top 45 settlements in the gazetteer ordered by peak documented population, illustrating the primacy of the dynastic capitals, commandery seats and maritime trade hubs.

```{r tab-top45, results='asis'}
fmt_coord <- function (x) gsub("[.]", ",", format(round(as.numeric(x), 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE))

get_pop_str <- function (e, y) {
  v <- e[["population"]][[y]]
  if (is.null(v)) return("-")
  viscount_fmt_pop(v)
}

peaks <- vapply(sett_data, function (e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
ord <- order(peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_n <- min(45L, length(ord))

rows <- lapply(sett_data[ord[seq_len(top_n)]], function (e) {
  yrs <- as.integer(names(e[["population"]]))
  pks <- as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))
  pk_y <- names(e[["population"]])[which.max(pks)]
  pk_y_str <- if (as.numeric(pk_y) < 0) paste0(abs(as.numeric(pk_y)), "BC") else paste0(pk_y, "AD")
  pk_v <- max(pks)
  reg_label <- if (e[["region_id"]] %in% names(reg_names)) reg_names[[e[["region_id"]]]] else e[["region_id"]]
  span_min <- if (min(yrs) < 0) paste0(abs(min(yrs)), "BC") else paste0(min(yrs), "AD")
  span_max <- if (max(yrs) < 0) paste0(abs(max(yrs)), "BC") else paste0(max(yrs), "AD")
  data.frame(
    Settlement = e[["name"]],
    Province = reg_label,
    Coords = paste0(fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[1]]), ", ", fmt_coord(e[["coords"]][[2]])),
    Span = paste0(span_min, "-", span_max),
    P2 = get_pop_str(e, "2"),
    P400 = get_pop_str(e, "400"),
    P668 = get_pop_str(e, "668"),
    Peak = paste0(viscount_fmt_pop(pk_v), " (", pk_y_str, ")"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
top_df <- do.call(rbind, rows)
rownames(top_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  top_df,
  "Top 45 settlements in early historical Korea ordered by peak documented population (n=209 total sites).",
  c("Settlement", "Territory", "Lat, Lon", "Span", "2AD", "400AD", "668AD", "Peak (Year)"),
  list(label = "tab:top45-korea", font_size = "scriptsize", max_rows_per_page = 26L)
)
```

## Sub-Regional Distribution and Ledger Exclusions

Table \ref{tab:regsum-korea} summarises the distribution of settlements across all eight macro-regions alongside their leading urban centres. The Han-Geum basin leads all territories with forty-one catalogued settlements, followed by Yeongsan-Honam (thirty-one), Gyeongbuk-Gyeongju (thirty-one), Lower Nakdong (twenty-seven), Pyongan-Taedong (twenty-seven) and Hwanghae-Imjin (twenty-six). Table \ref{tab:excluded-korea} details the leading 30 of 507 excluded candidate entries in the regional source ledger.

```{r tab-regsum, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)

sum_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function (rk) {
  sub_e <- Filter(function (e) identical(e[["region_id"]], rk), sett_data)
  max_nm <- "-"
  if (length(sub_e) > 0) {
    pks <- vapply(sub_e, function (e) max(as.numeric(unlist(e[["population"]]))), numeric(1))
    idx_m <- which.max(pks)
    pk_y <- names(sub_e[[idx_m]][["population"]])[which.max(as.numeric(unlist(sub_e[[idx_m]][["population"]])))]
    pk_y_str <- if (as.numeric(pk_y) < 0) paste0(abs(as.numeric(pk_y)), "BC") else paste0(pk_y, "AD")
    max_nm <- paste0(sub_e[[idx_m]][["name"]], " (", viscount_fmt_pop(pks[idx_m]), ", ", pk_y_str, ")")
  }
  reg_short <- sub("^[0-9]+\\.\\s*", "", mod_data$regions[[rk]]$name)
  data.frame(
    Territory = gsub("&", "and", reg_short, fixed = TRUE),
    Sites = as.character(length(sub_e)),
    Lead = max_nm,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
sum_df <- do.call(rbind, sum_rows)
rownames(sum_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  sum_df,
  "Settlement counts and leading urban citadels across the eight macro-regions (209 total sites).",
  c("Territory", "Catalogued Sites", "Leading Centre (Peak)"),
  list(label = "tab:regsum-korea", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

```{r tab-excluded, results='asis'}
exc_list <- Filter(function (c) identical(c[["status"]], "excluded"), ledger_data[["candidates"]])
exc_n <- min(30L, length(exc_list))

exc_rows <- lapply(exc_list[seq_len(exc_n)], function (c) {
  just <- as.character(c[["justification"]])
  just <- gsub("([0-9]+)\\.([0-9]+)\\s*km", "\\1,\\2 km", just, perl = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    Candidate = c[["name"]],
    Territory = c[["country"]],
    Category = "Duplicate alias",
    Justification = just,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
exc_df <- do.call(rbind, exc_rows)
rownames(exc_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  exc_df,
  "Leading 30 of 507 excluded candidate entries in the early Korea source ledger, consolidated into canonical settlements.",
  c("Candidate", "Territory", "Classification", "Consolidation Justification"),
  list(label = "tab:excluded-korea", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Limitations

Two spatial factors affect settlement aggregation in this gazetteer. First, early Korean historical capitals comprised dispersed multi-citadel complexes rather than single bounded circuits: Hanseong comprised both Pungnaptoseong and Mongchontoseong; Buyeo comprised Busosanseong, Naseong and royal palace pavilions; and Pyongyang comprised Anhak Palace, Daeseongsanseong and the later Janganseong wall system [@Barnes2015Archaeology; @Hong2018Cultural]. These contiguous and functionally interdependent features are consolidated into single unified metropolitan entries with distinct component records to avoid double-counting contiguous urban populations. Second, minor fortified outposts (*bo*) and watchtowers lacking civilian market settlements are excluded from the gazetteer and absorbed into regional agrarian totals [@Barnes2015Archaeology].
